title: Trade Negotiations
outcomes: Classify regional trade agreements from unilateral preferences to economic and monetary union and explain why FTAs need rules of origin.
Explain why GATT lost relevance and how the Uruguay Round created the WTO.
Describe the WTO's objectives, functions, three-tier structure, membership and guiding principles (MFN, national treatment, binding, fair competition, development).
Outline the main WTO agreements and the Doha Round, and the concerns of developing countries.

meta.exam_tip: Facts and principles: 164 members (117 developing), Ministerial Conference every two years, Uruguay Round 1986–1993 (123 countries), Doha November 2001 (9th round, 4th Ministerial). FTA vs customs union, MFN vs national treatment are favourites.

concepts.title: Trade negotiations and regional trade agreements (RTAs)
body: Trade negotiations are bargaining processes between governments with competing aims — one side seeks market access through lower tariffs, the other seeks protection for its industries. Lobbies, pressure groups and NGOs also influence the outcome. The material notes that India was part of 19 concluded agreements and negotiating over two dozen more; and that 2020 saw Brexit and the USMCA (successor to NAFTA), amid the US–China trade war and the pandemic.

An RTA is a treaty between two or more governments setting trade rules for all signatories, formed to reduce barriers among members. Members need not be in the same geographical region. The material counts 339 RTAs in force on 1 February 2021.

Types, from shallow to deep: unilateral (one-way incentives, e.g. GSP), bilateral (two countries or blocs), regional preferential trade agreements (reciprocal, reduced barriers for members), then a trading bloc, a free trade area, a customs union, a common market and finally an economic and monetary union.

blocks.title: Types of trade agreement — from shallow to deep integration

concepts.analogy: Integration is like a friendship deepening: a one-way favour, then mutual discounts, then free entry to each other's homes, then a shared front door, then a joint bank account.
concepts.work: Each new agreement changes duty rates, rules of origin and compliance paperwork. CAs advising importers and exporters map which agreement gives the best duty and what documentation it needs.

concepts.title: Free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary union
body: Free trade area (FTA): members remove all tariffs and quotas on trade among themselves but each keeps its own, independent tariff on imports from outside. Example: the ASEAN–India FTA (ten ASEAN states and India), in force from 1 August 2005.

Customs union: free trade among members PLUS a common external tariff on non-members — so the same duty applies wherever goods enter the union. Because outsiders face a higher duty than members, it technically departs from MFN. Examples: the EU (27 members, one customs territory), GCC, MERCOSUR.
Common market: a customs union plus free movement of factors of production (labour, capital) and some harmonisation of commercial and financial laws.
Economic and monetary union: a common market with a single currency, which requires strong convergence of macroeconomic policies — e.g. the European Union countries using a single currency.
concepts.analogy: FTA: neighbours stop charging each other entry fees but each keeps its own gate rules for strangers. Customs union: they build one common gate with one fee.
concepts.work: Rules-of-origin compliance exists because of FTAs; customs unions avoid it. Knowing which a partner group is tells a CA how much origin documentation a client needs.

concepts.title: GATT and why it lost relevance
body: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade covers international trade in goods. Within the WTO, the Council for Trade in Goods (Goods Council), made up of all members, oversees it through 10 committees (agriculture, market access, subsidies, anti-dumping and others), together with a working party on state-trading enterprises and the committee for the IT Agreement.
GATT provided the rules for most world trade from 1948 to 1994 and held eight rounds that cut tariffs substantially.

Why it lost relevance by the 1980s: unsuited to a complex, globalising world; investment had grown hugely; services and intellectual property were outside it; merchandise trade had outgrown it; its ambiguities could be exploited; agricultural liberalisation had failed; its institutions and dispute settlement were weak; and it was not a treaty, so it bound nations only to the extent it did not clash with domestic law.
concepts.analogy: GATT was a gentlemen's club rulebook written for goods; by the 1980s the members were also trading services and ideas, and the club had no proper referee.
concepts.work: Many tariff concessions an importer relies on today trace back to GATT rounds; knowing the history helps interpret bound rates in the tariff schedule.

concepts.title: The Uruguay Round and the birth of the WTO
body: Launched at Punta del Este, Uruguay in September 1986 and due to finish by December 1990, the Round stalled — especially over agriculture — and was completed only in December 1993 after seven years. It was the eighth, the most ambitious and the largest round, with 123 participating countries.

Fifteen negotiating groups covered tariffs, non-tariff barriers, tropical and natural-resource products, textiles and clothing, agriculture, safeguards against import surges, subsidies and countervailing duties, trade-related intellectual property, trade-related investment, services, and the GATT system itself (dispute settlement, implementation of Tokyo Round codes, especially anti-dumping).

The agreement was signed by most countries on 15 April 1994. It created the World Trade Organization, a single institutional framework encompassing GATT as modified by the Round — the biggest reform of the world trading system since the Second World War.

blocks.title: GATT to WTO — key dates

concepts.analogy: The Uruguay Round turned a loose club rulebook into a full constitution with a court — the WTO.
concepts.work: TRIPS, GATS, SPS and TBT — all born in this Round — shape patent costs, service exports and product compliance for Indian businesses today.

concepts.title: The WTO: objectives, functions and structure
body: The WTO is the only global organisation dealing with the rules of trade between nations. Its principal aim is to help trade flow smoothly, freely, fairly and predictably.

Six key objectives: set and enforce rules for international trade; provide a forum for negotiating and monitoring further liberalisation; resolve trade disputes; make decision-making more transparent; cooperate with other international economic institutions; and help developing countries benefit fully. The preamble speaks of raising living standards, full employment, growing real income and effective demand, and expanding production of and trade in goods and services.
Functions: forum for negotiations, administering agreements, reviewing national trade policies, technical assistance and training for developing countries, cooperation with other organisations.

Structure (three tiers): the Ministerial Conference — the top body, meeting at least once every two years; the General Council — meets several times a year in Geneva and also sits in two other capacities — as the body that settles disputes (DSB) and the body that reviews trade policies (TPRB); then the Goods, Services and TRIPS Councils reporting to it. A Secretariat in Geneva, headed by a Director-General, supports the work.

Membership (as given in the material): 164 members in all — 117 of them developing countries or separate customs territories; together about 95% of world trade; around 24 others negotiating to join. (Real-world note: Comoros and Timor-Leste joined in 2024, taking membership to 166; for the exam, quote the material's figure of 164 unless 166 is the only matching option.) Over three-quarters of members are developing or transition economies.
concepts.analogy: Ministerial Conference = the parliament that meets every two years; General Council = the cabinet that meets often; specialised councils = ministries; Secretariat = civil service.
concepts.work: When India disputes another country's duties (or is challenged), the case goes to the Dispute Settlement Body. Industry bodies — with CA support on data — feed into these cases.

concepts.title: Guiding principles of the WTO
body: Trade without discrimination — (1) Most-favoured-nation: a favour to one member (e.g. a lower duty) must go to all members. It is Article I of GATT, Article 2 of GATS and Article 4 of TRIPS. Exceptions under strict conditions: FTAs/customs unions, special market access for developing countries, barriers against unfairly traded goods, limited cases in services. (2) National treatment: imported and local goods, services and IP must be treated equally once the import has entered the market (GATT Article 3, GATS Article 17, TRIPS Article 3); a customs duty at the border is therefore not a violation.
Freer trade gradually through negotiation — "progressive liberalisation", with longer periods for developing countries.

Predictability through binding and transparency — bound tariffs are ceilings; changing them needs negotiation and possibly compensation. The Uruguay Round raised the share of trade under bindings; in agriculture 100% of products now have bound tariffs. Quotas are discouraged; rules must be published and notified; the Trade Policy Review Mechanism keeps watch.

Promoting fair competition — the WTO is better described as a system of rules for open, fair and undistorted competition than as a pure "free trade" body: tariffs and, in limited cases, other protection are allowed; rules on dumping and subsidies define unfair trade.

Encouraging development and economic reform — flexibility, transition periods and special assistance for developing and least-developed countries, including duty-free and quota-free access for almost all products from LDCs in developed markets.
concepts.analogy: MFN: "If I give one friend a discount, every friend gets it." National treatment: "Once you are inside my shop, you are treated like family."
concepts.work: Before a client lobbies for a duty hike, a CA checks the bound rate — the government cannot go above it without compensating partners.

concepts.title: WTO agreements and the Doha Round
body: Main agreements: Agriculture (market access, domestic support, export subsidies); SPS; Textiles and Clothing (replaced the Multi-Fibre Arrangement in force since 1974, integrating textiles into GATT over 10 years); TBT; TRIMs (no local-content or trade-balancing requirements inconsistent with national treatment and the ban on quantitative restrictions); Anti-Dumping; Customs Valuation; Pre-shipment Inspection; Rules of Origin; Import Licensing; Subsidies & Countervailing Measures (SCM); Safeguards; GATS (services: MFN, transparency, sector commitments); TRIPS (MFN and national treatment for copyright, trademarks, geographical indications, designs, patents, IC layouts, undisclosed information, with enforcement); Dispute Settlement Understanding; Trade Policy Review Mechanism; and plurilateral agreements (civil aircraft, government procurement) signed by only some members.

The Doha Round (Doha Development Agenda): the ninth round since the Second World War, launched at the WTO's 4th Ministerial Conference in Doha, Qatar in November 2001. It covers about 20 areas — agriculture, services, non-agricultural market access (NAMA), trade facilitation, environment, geographical indications and other IP issues. Agriculture was the most controversial topic, and progress has been slow.

Issues and criticism: slow multilateral talks, uncertainty from the spread of RTAs, limited liberalisation, and developing-country concerns — protectionism and limited market access in developed countries, implementation difficulties, a north–south divide, very high tariffs and tariff escalation on their products, erosion of preferences.

The material also notes WTO monitoring of G20 economies (2022): export restrictions on food, feed and fertiliser added to price volatility, and the Director-General urged G20 members to keep markets open and predictable.
concepts.analogy: The WTO agreements are chapters of one rulebook; the Doha Round is the long-running attempt to write the next edition.
concepts.work: TRIPS shapes patent and licensing costs for pharma clients; GATS commitments shape whether Indian CA firms can serve clients abroad; customs valuation rules decide the assessable value on which duty is paid.

solution.title: Types of trade agreement — from shallow to deep integration

solution.text: Order: preferential trade agreement → free trade area → customs union → common market → economic and monetary union. Each step adds: tariffs reduced → tariffs removed → common external tariff → free factor movement and harmonised rules → single currency with policy convergence.

illustrations.title: Most-favoured-nation treatment with numbers
illustrations.q: Country A (a WTO member) charges 12% on imported bicycles from all WTO members. After talks with Country B it wants to charge B only 8%. A and B are NOT in a free trade area or customs union. What must A do, and how does this affect a ₹5,00,000 consignment from Country C, another WTO member?

solution.provision: MFN (Article I of GATT): a favour granted to one WTO member — such as a lower duty — must be extended immediately to all other WTO members for like products. Exceptions exist for FTAs/customs unions, special access for developing countries, and measures against unfair trade.
solution.facts: A wants to lower its bicycle duty for B from 12% to 8%. A and B have no FTA or customs union; C is also a WTO member.
solution.analysis: No exception applies, so the 8% rate must be given to C too. Duty on C's consignment: before 12% × 5,00,000 = ₹60,000; after 8% × 5,00,000 = ₹40,000.
solution.conclusion: A must apply 8% to all WTO members. C's exporter saves ₹20,000 per such consignment — every tariff cut becomes multilateral.

checks.label: duty on C before at MFN 12%
duty on C after the cut is extended to all

illustrations.title: Why an FTA needs rules of origin but a customs union does not
illustrations.q: X and Y form a free trade area. On imports of a ₹1,000 gadget from an outside country, X charges 5% and Y charges 20%. (a) What duty is paid if the gadget enters Y directly, and if it enters through X and then moves duty-free to Y? (b) What changes if X and Y form a customs union with a common external tariff of 12%?

head: Route
Working
Duty (₹)
rows: FTA — into X, then duty-free to Y
Incentive to deflect trade through X
Customs union — entry through either member

solution.text: In an FTA each member keeps its own external tariff, so importers would route goods through the low-duty member (trade deflection). Rules of origin stop this: only goods originating in the FTA get duty-free movement. In a customs union the same tariff applies wherever the goods enter, so there is no incentive to deflect.

checks.label: duty under a common external tariff of 12%

illustrations.title: National treatment: border duty vs internal tax
illustrations.q: Country M charges 10% customs duty on imported soap. Inside the country it also levies a sales tax of 18% on imported soap but 12% on locally made soap of the same kind. A ₹200 bar is sold in each case. Does either measure violate national treatment?

solution.provision: National treatment (GATT Article 3, GATS Article 17, TRIPS Article 3): once foreign goods have entered the market, they must be treated no less favourably than like domestic goods. It applies only after entry, so a customs duty at the border is not a violation.
solution.facts: Customs duty 10% at the border; internal tax ₹36 on an imported bar against ₹24 on a local bar.
solution.analysis: The customs duty is charged at entry — allowed (subject to bound rates). The sales tax discriminates after entry: the imported bar bears ₹12 more tax than a like local bar.
solution.conclusion: The 10% customs duty is permitted; the higher internal tax on imported soap violates national treatment.

checks.label: internal tax on imported soap at 18%
internal tax on local soap at 12%

jobs.title: Choosing the cheapest legal route under trade agreements
jobs.role: CA in industry (supply-chain finance, auto-components maker)
jobs.situation: You source an alloy from Thailand. Duty options: MFN rate, or the ASEAN–India FTA rate if the supplier provides a valid certificate of origin.
steps: Confirm the product meets the FTA's origin criteria (value addition / change in tariff classification).
Compare landed cost under MFN and FTA rates.
Keep origin documents for the period required for customs verification.
Do not route non-originating goods through an FTA partner — that is exactly what rules of origin prevent.
jobs.takeaway: FTAs reward compliance: duty savings depend on proving origin.
jobs.think: Why would the same alloy from China not get the ASEAN–India rate even if shipped via Thailand?
jobs.answer: Because it does not originate in an FTA member; merely passing through Thailand does not confer origin, so the MFN rate applies.

jobs.title: Explaining a WTO dispute to a board
jobs.situation: A trading partner has raised duty on your members' product above its bound rate.
steps: Check the partner's bound rate in its WTO schedule.
Raising an applied rate above the bound rate breaches its commitment unless it negotiated and compensated partners.
Brief the government (which alone can bring a WTO case) with trade-loss data.
Meanwhile, explore FTA markets with lower duties.
jobs.takeaway: Binding gives exporters legal certainty; the Dispute Settlement Body enforces it.

mcqs.explain: 339 RTAs; 164 is WTO membership; 123 countries in the Uruguay Round; 117 developing members.

mcqs.explain: GSP is unilateral and non-reciprocal.

mcqs.explain: A common external tariff would make it a customs union.

mcqs.explain: Both remove internal tariffs; only a customs union adds a common external tariff.

mcqs.explain: Common market = customs union + factor mobility.

mcqs.explain: The final stage of integration.

Members charge each other higher duties
mcqs.explain: Members get zero duty; non-members pay the common external tariff.

mcqs.q: In a free trade area, X charges 6% and Y charges 18% on a ₹2,000 good from outside. How much duty can an importer avoid by entering through X instead of Y (if there are no rules of origin)?
mcqs.explain: Y: 18% × 2,000 = 360; X: 6% × 2,000 = 120; difference ₹240 — trade deflection, prevented by rules of origin.

mcqs.q: GATT covered international trade in:
mcqs.explain: Services (GATS) and IP (TRIPS) came with the WTO.

options: It covered services and intellectual property comprehensively
Its dispute settlement system was weak
mcqs.explain: GATT did NOT cover services and IP — that was a weakness.

mcqs.q: GATT provided the rules for most of world trade for about:
mcqs.explain: From 1948 to 1994.

mcqs.q: The Uruguay Round was launched in:
mcqs.explain: Launched at Punta del Este in September 1986; completed December 1993; signed 15 April 1994.

mcqs.q: How many countries participated in the Uruguay Round?
mcqs.explain: 123 countries — the largest round.

mcqs.q: The Uruguay Round was the ___ round of multilateral trade negotiations under GATT.
mcqs.explain: The eighth and last GATT round; Doha is the ninth since the Second World War.

mcqs.q: The most controversial issue that delayed the Uruguay Round was:
mcqs.explain: Heated controversies over agriculture.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the six key objectives of the WTO?
options: Fixing exchange rates of member countries
Providing a forum for negotiating further liberalisation
Helping developing countries benefit from trade
mcqs.explain: Exchange rates are not a WTO objective.

mcqs.q: The highest decision-making body of the WTO is the:
mcqs.explain: It meets at least once every two years.

mcqs.q: The WTO Ministerial Conference meets at least once every:
mcqs.explain: The General Council meets several times a year in between.

mcqs.q: The WTO General Council also meets as the:
options: Dispute Settlement Body and Trade Policy Review Body
mcqs.explain: One body, three hats.

mcqs.explain: 164 members in total as per the material; 117 of them are developing countries or separate customs territories. (Membership became 166 in 2024 with Comoros and Timor-Leste.)

mcqs.explain: Headed by a Director-General.

Imported goods must be taxed like domestic goods after entry

mcqs.explain: The second option describes national treatment.

mcqs.q: MFN appears as Article I of:
mcqs.explain: GATT Article I; in GATS it is Article 2, in TRIPS Article 4.

mcqs.q: Charging customs duty on an import, while no equivalent tax is charged on a like local product:
options: Does not violate national treatment, as it applies only after entry
mcqs.explain: National treatment applies once goods have entered the market.

mcqs.explain: MFN: the 7% must be extended to all members — 7% × 3,00,000 = ₹21,000.

mcqs.q: Which WTO principle is served by "binding" tariffs?
mcqs.explain: Bindings are ceilings that give traders certainty.

mcqs.q: The share of agricultural products with bound tariffs after the Uruguay Round is:
mcqs.explain: All agricultural products now have bound tariffs.

A pure free-trade institution that bans all tariffs
A body that fixes world prices

mcqs.explain: The MFA had been in force since 1974; ATC integrated textiles into GATT over 10 years.

mcqs.explain: Trade-Related Investment Measures.

mcqs.explain: Multilateral agreements bind all members.

mcqs.explain: Doha, Qatar — the ninth round since the Second World War.

mcqs.q: The most controversial topic in the Doha agenda was:
mcqs.explain: As in the Uruguay Round.

questions.q: Describe the three-tier decision-making structure of the WTO.

items: Top tier — Ministerial Conference: highest authority; can decide on any matter under any multilateral agreement; meets at least once every two years.
Second tier — General Council: meets several times a year in Geneva; doubles up as the Dispute Settlement Body and as the Trade Policy Review Body.
Third tier — Councils for Trade in Goods, Trade in Services and TRIPS: report to the General Council and oversee their agreements, assisted by committees and working groups.
Support — the Secretariat in Geneva headed by the Director-General.

viva.q: Why did GATT lose its relevance and give way to the WTO?
viva.model: GATT covered only trade in goods, so services, intellectual property and investment were outside it. It was not a treaty, its dispute settlement and institutions were weak, its ambiguities were exploited and agricultural liberalisation had failed. So the Uruguay Round created the WTO as a stronger, permanent organisation.

points.pt: Did not cover services, intellectual property or investment

viva.q: Describe the decision-making structure of the WTO.
viva.model: The WTO has a three-tier structure. At the top is the Ministerial Conference, which meets at least once every two years. Next is the General Council in Geneva, which also sits as the Dispute Settlement Body and the Trade Policy Review Body. Below it are the Goods, Services and TRIPS Councils. A Secretariat headed by the Director-General supports them.

viva.model: The Doha Round, formally the Doha Development Agenda, is the ninth round of multilateral trade talks since the Second World War. It began in November 2001 at the fourth WTO Ministerial Conference, held in Doha, Qatar, and covers about twenty areas such as agriculture, services, non-agricultural market access and trade facilitation. Agriculture has been the most controversial issue.

cases.title: Three neighbours plan a trade pact
cases.case: Aurelia, Brenna and Corvia are WTO members. They plan to remove all duties on trade among themselves. Aurelia wants each country to keep its own duties on outsiders (Aurelia 5%, Brenna 12%, Corvia 20% on electronics). Brenna proposes a single 12% duty on outsiders and, later, free movement of workers and capital. Separately, Corvia wants to give Dravia (a WTO member outside the pact) a special 8% duty on electronics while all others pay 20%. Corvia also taxes imported electronics at 15% inside the country, against 10% on local electronics.

mcqs.q: Aurelia's proposal describes a:
mcqs.explain: Own external tariffs = FTA.

mcqs.q: Brenna's full proposal (single external duty, then free factor movement) leads ultimately to a:
mcqs.explain: Common external tariff → customs union; + factor mobility → common market.

mcqs.q: Under Aurelia's plan, how much duty is avoided on ₹50,000 of outside electronics entering through Aurelia instead of Corvia, if there were no rules of origin?
mcqs.explain: Corvia 20% = 10,000; Aurelia 5% = 2,500; difference ₹7,500.

mcqs.q: Corvia's special 8% rate for Dravia alone would violate:
mcqs.explain: Dravia is outside any FTA with Corvia, so the favour must go to all WTO members.

mcqs.q: Corvia's 15% internal tax on imported vs 10% on local electronics violates:
options: Nothing, as it is an internal tax
mcqs.explain: Discrimination after entry breaches national treatment.
